Chaque matin, alors que bon nombre de Qu: Every morning, as many Quebecers head off to work, they take on a complex task that nonetheless often goes unnoticed: they look after their children throughout the day. “They,” because these are mostly women. Many are immigrants. In this series, we present portraits of the educators and caregivers who work in Quebec schools.
Fin d’une journée de juin dans un café d: Late on a June day, in a Montréal café, we meet Amina*. The sky can't make up its mind: it rains, it stops raining, and this dance drags on all day. She arrives right on time, carrying a pretty umbrella. But we'll need a few minutes before we can begin talking. The children from the school across the street come into the café with their parents. They keep coming over to say hello to Amina, even after spending the whole day with her. They adore her.
Il faut dire qu’elle est partout dans l’: She is, it must be said, everywhere at the public school where she has worked for four years as a childcare educator. Her voice is deep, her words gentle. She moves with grace and lightness. Her very small frame is at odds with the presence she gives off: the moment she walks into the café, you feel it. She has been doing this job for fourteen years, and she takes it very seriously. In her home country, Morocco, she was a French teacher for fifteen years, after which she retired and moved to Quebec. After having the equivalencies for her studies recognized, she earned a college diploma (DEC), which allows her to hold this position.
En s'installant à Montréal, Amina prend: When she settled in Montréal, Amina made the decision to stay home with her two children. At the time, she was married, and her husband had a good job. “It was a choice. I didn't want to leave [my girls] to go to work.” After a few years, she was ready to return to the job market and took a position she enjoyed, though it had nothing to do with children. As time went on, Amina had to face the facts: she missed that contact. A lot.
Elle devient donc éducatrice, un poste q: So she became an educator, a job she has no intention of leaving. “As long as I'm healthy, I'll work,” she says, with her frank, warm smile. That may sound easy to say, but you have to spend a whole day working with Grade 2 students to truly understand what it involves.
À 68 ans aujourd’hui, Amina fait trois b: Now 68, Amina works three shifts at the school. She arrives at 7 a.m. and leaves at 6 p.m. On pedagogical days, she also accompanies the children on metro or bus outings to every corner of the city.
S’occuper d’un groupe de 18 élèves penda: Looking after a group of 18 students for all those hours is exhausting, even for a younger person. But Amina never looks tired. She can come back from an outing to the park on a rainy day, as she did today, and then head to a café to answer all our questions.
Quand elle parle de son métier, Amina dé: When she talks about her work, Amina brims with enthusiasm. “Everything we do has a big impact on a child: our behaviour, our words, our voice. You can contribute very positively to their confidence, their self-esteem, their ability to help others. But you can also have a negative impact. Words leave a mark on children.”
Aujourd'hui, avec la pénurie de main-d'œ: Today, with the labour shortage in this field – as everywhere in Quebec's public education sector – she regrets the loosening of hiring criteria.
« J’aimerais qu’ils exigent un diplôme u: “I'd like them to require a university degree,” she says. “It saddens me that we don't give this the importance it deserves. That has to change if we want to offer quality service [to the schools of the Centre de Services Scolaires de Montréal].”
Elle nous montre un texte qu’elle a écri: She shows us a text she wrote a few years ago for a presentation to professionals in training: “Anyone can look after a child. The only requirements are to be 12 years old or older and able to watch over a child until the parent arrives. But our work as educators rests above all on the meaningful relationship we build with children. It is through this relationship that we pass on values of respect, generosity, sharing, mutual aid, empathy and open-mindedness. Being an educator means passing on skills; it also means passing on know-how and ways of being.” She is deeply committed to these values; you can see it. She speaks with delight about the time shared with the children, those little moments that can go unnoticed in a long school day but are also part of the little ones' lives.
À l’école, les élèves viennent la voir :: At school, the students come to find her: “Look at my new skirt, Amina.” “Come give me a hug, Amina.” She knows everyone's name.
C'est le cas d’une petite fille qui a de: Take the case of a little girl who has trouble adjusting. At the start of the year, the girl often squabbled with her classmates. She had a hard time making friends. At recess, she would often cry in a corner. “Nobody could figure out what was happening to her,” says Nassima, another educator at the school. “She was lucky to have Amina this year,” she says.
Car Amina l’a pris sous son aile. « Je t: Because Amina took her under her wing. “I'm working hard to see a change in this little girl. For me, the children who struggle are the ones who most need us to be there for them. That's where I can make a difference.”
Quelques jours avant la fin de l’année s: A few days before the end of the school year, the little girl is playing in the schoolyard with another girl. They whisper secrets to each other and laugh as they look at a piece of cardboard covered in drawings that one brought for the other. She's no longer crying in her corner; she even has a beautiful smile on her face. “It's a big difference from the beginning of the year!” says Nassima.
« Amina est quelqu’un d’exemplaire », di: “Amina is exemplary,” says Nassima. “What I like most about her is how she handles situations and discipline: she provides structure and is very firm, but at the same time she always stays kind.” When she needs the children to listen, Amina explains the rules and the consequences to them, “and I finish with a compliment,” she says.
Élevée au sein d’une famille de la class: Raised in a middle-class family in Morocco, Amina is a woman who knows what she wants. After a year of studying law in her country, she flew to France, where she met her future husband. He was very active in politics at the time.
Le jeune couple retourne au Maroc et par: The young couple returned to Morocco and helped found a left-wing party opposed to the Moroccan regime of the day. On this subject, she prefers to remain discreet, “out of respect for the other activists” who went to prison for their political activities. Her husband, for one.
Même si elle estime avoir eu de la « cha: Even though she considers herself to have been “lucky,” being seen as a rebel in that period was not easy, she explains, and even more so when you're a woman. But that is Amina's nature: she is not the type to sit back with her arms crossed and say nothing.
À l’époque, elle fait aussi partie d’une: At the time, she was also part of an association fighting for women's rights in her country. When the situation calmed down, her husband was released, and after years of a more peaceful life, the couple decided to leave. “We told ourselves it was time to go looking for something else.” They already had a child.
« Ce n’était pas une fuite, c’était un c: “It wasn't an escape, it was a choice,” she clarifies. “We chose Quebec because we wanted a French-speaking place to settle. It was already hard enough to leave everything behind without adding a language we don't speak, like English.” Fortunately for Amina and her little family, the experience of immigrating was not traumatic, but she also holds tightly to her roots.
Elle n’oublie pas d’où elle vient, et fa: She doesn't forget where she comes from, and does everything she can so that her children don't forget either. In fact, she took care to pass Arabic on to her eldest daughter. The youngest, however, had a weaker command of the language… until an episode that marked the whole family's life: the night before Amina left for a vacation in Morocco, her youngest confided in her: “Mom, I want to go with you. I want to go see.”
« Cela paraissait impossible ! Trouver l: “It seemed impossible! Finding a ticket from one day to the next, preparing for the trip…” Yet the next day, her 18-year-old daughter left with her mother, “by some miracle,” Amina recalls. Another major surprise: the young woman loved her country of origin so much that she decided to stay.
Amina appelle alors sa patronne au Québe: Amina then called her boss in Quebec to ask for an unpaid leave. That is how she and her daughter spent an entire year rediscovering their language and their culture. “Before, my daughter felt a little left out of our family conversations. After that year, she was very proud. And she has kept that.”
Pour Amina il est important de préserver: For Amina, it is important to preserve origins and stories. “In my community, I see a lot of young people who don't speak the language. They have no connection to their culture, they don't know where they come from.”
Amina ne cesse de nourrir des rêves pour: Amina never stops nurturing dreams for the children around her and for her community. We don't know whether those dreams will come true. But after everything we know about her, there is hope. Sometimes, hope wears a lovely sun.
